title: Why Students Tattle And What To Do About It
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin reframes student tattling not as an annoying personality trait but as a predictable response to a teacher who either lacks a functioning classroom management plan or fails to consistently enforce the one they have. He argues that students tattle because they need the teacher to protect their right to learn and enjoy school, and that discouraging tattling without fixing the underlying enforcement gap leaves students with no legitimate outlet when a classmate interferes with them. His five-step solution includes reevaluating the classroom management plan to ensure it covers all disruptive behaviors, consistently enforcing consequences, actively encouraging students to report problems privately, dropping the stigmatizing word "tattling," and building in a loophole for behaviors, like bullying, that call for immediate escalation. The piece closes by urging teachers to embrace reporting rather than shut it down.
points: Tattling is reframed as a predictable symptom of inconsistent rule enforcement, not a student character flaw.
Consistently enforcing consequences for every rule violation is said to eliminate roughly 90% of tattling.
Discouraging tattling without fixing enforcement leaves students without a legitimate way to report real problems.
Dropping the stigmatizing label "tattling" and instead framing reports as a duty reduces the fear of being marginalized for speaking up.
A built-in "loophole" for serious issues like bullying should allow immediate escalation of consequences.
quotes: There is a reason students tattle. But it has nothing to do with them. They are not the problem. They’re merely doing what they feel like they must do. The problem is with you, their teacher.
Tattling is the result of teachers not fulfilling their most important responsibility: to protect every student’s right to learn and enjoy school without interference.

Your classroom management plan isn't worth the poster it's printed on if you don't follow it. For every rule that is broken, enforce a consequence without a second thought. This simple step removes 90% of tattling.
Frequently remind your class that it’s your job to protect their right to learn and enjoy school. If anyone interferes with that right, you want to know about it.
But tattling has a negative connotation. It discourages students from coming to you with a legitimate problem for fear they’ll be made fun or marginalized for it.
If someone is bothering them, bullying them, or otherwise interfering with learning, they have an obligation to tell you. You must know. It’s your job to know.
